stem: An 11-month-old boy is brought to the pediatrician for a follow-up visit. He has a history of three episodes of acute otitis media and one episode of bronchiolitis requiring hospitalization in the past six months. The mother also notes that the child has an itchy, scaly rash on his cheeks and has had several episodes of wheezing. Vitals are: temperature 36.7°C, pulse 110/min, respiratory rate 28/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Physical examination reveals mild erythematous, scaly plaques on both cheeks and bilateral wheezing on auscultation. Laboratory studies show a serum IgG level of 3.2 g/L (Normal for age: 4.0–12.0 g/L), while IgM and IgA levels are at the lower end of the normal range. A trial of vaccination with tetanus toxoid is performed, and the subsequent IgG titer shows a robust, normal increase.
lead_in: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The patient presents with recurrent respiratory infections, atopic features (eczema, wheezing), and a low serum IgG level at 11 months of age. The key diagnostic finding is the normal antibody response to the tetanus toxoid vaccine. This demonstrates that the patient's B cells are functional and capable of producing antibodies, which is characteristic of transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy (THI). In THI, there is a delayed synthesis of IgG, causing a prolonged nadir beyond the typical 6-month mark, but it eventually resolves spontaneously. Common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) also presents with low IgG, but patients with CVID fail to produce a normal antibody response to vaccines. X-linked agammaglobulinemia (E) would show severely low levels of all immunoglobulin classes and a lack of B cells on flow cytometry. Hyper-IgM syndrome (B) would typically feature elevated or normal IgM with low IgG and IgA. Selective IgA deficiency (C) would show isolated low IgA with normal IgG.
teaching_point: Transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy is characterized by low serum IgG and recurrent infections in infants, but it is distinguished from more severe immunodeficiencies by a normal antibody response to vaccinations.

distractor_rationale.A: CVID presents with low IgG and a failure to mount a normal antibody response to vaccines.
distractor_rationale.B: Presents with low IgG/IgA but normal or high IgM and failure to class-switch.
distractor_rationale.C: Involves isolated low IgA levels, not isolated low IgG.
distractor_rationale.D: Correct: Low IgG in an infant with a preserved ability to respond to vaccines.
distractor_rationale.E: Presents earlier (usually >6 months) with absent B cells and very low levels of all immunoglobulins.
